content:
In the past few days, two reports have pointed to different ways Apple could grow its profits by boosting services revenue.

In my view, Apple absolutely should adopt the first approach, but should not adopt the second — and it seems Phil Schiller may well agree with that view…

Let me first summarise the content of these two reports.

Home security and monitoring services

On Friday, Bloomberg reported that Apple may be planning to launch a brand-new home security and monitoring service, expected to roll out alongside some of the new home hardware we have been waiting for.

Squeezing more revenue from the App Store

Bloomberg's second report on Sunday indicated that Apple is exploring various ways to squeeze more revenue and profit from the App Store.

Apple should not adopt the latter approach

On the contrary, I believe the second approach would be a very serious mistake.

Apple's effective monopoly over iPhone app sales is already being questioned by regulators around the world. In most countries, if you want to sell iPhone apps, you must do so through the official App Store, with no choice whatsoever but to accept the terms Apple sets, leaving no room to negotiate.

I understand many people feel that no one is forcing you to buy an iPhone or develop apps for it, but that view does not align with how even the most laissez-faire capitalism actually works in practice: even in the United States, antitrust laws have been in place since 1890. Once you reach a certain level of market dominance, you become subject to behavioural constraints to ensure you do not abuse that position.

Trying to squeeze more money out of the App Store runs counter to the philosophy of "skating to where the puck is going" — and reportedly Phil Schiller agrees with this. Bloomberg noted that this is one of the reasons he has stepped back from the front lines.

Innovative services are the right direction

Instead, Apple should roll out brand-new, innovative services that customers are happy to pay for. I can easily see the value of Apple offering a home security monitoring service.

I stated back in 2024 that developing its own smart home cameras would be one of the wisest moves the company could make. At the time, I expressed the same view about the widely rumored Apple smart doorbell. Adding an optional service bundle to security products makes complete sense, for two reasons.

First, all the privacy reasons I have previously mentioned apply. HomeKit Secure Video has already done a great deal to safeguard the privacy of security camera footage. If there is one company I would trust to run AI analysis on security camera footage, it is Apple.

Second, Apple is of course the company best positioned to fully integrate security hardware and services within the HomeKit ecosystem. I firmly believe there are many other areas where Apple could offer similar advantages.

For me, the key point is that Apple needs to treat services with the same attitude it applies to hardware — building outstanding products that customers willingly and happily pay for, rather than making money in ways that irritate customers, developers, and regulators.

What do you think? Feel free to share your views in the comments section.
